1. The animation shows how inflation erodes what a fixed income can buy. Three illustrative retirees each get the same 2% raise. Edna starts in Jan 1949, Ruth in Aug 2006 and Carl in Jan 1966. Each retiree's income is shown as a row of crates of goods. The label reads "crates at year 20 · same 2% raise". The footer says "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. At the start, all three rows are full and the same length. Over the 20 years the rows shrink by different amounts, based on what actual US consumer prices (CPI-U) did in each starting period. At year 20, Edna still has 10 crates. Ruth has about 9. Carl has only about 4.

3. The same 2% raise protects buying power very differently depending on when you retire and how fast prices rise. Edna's period had mild inflation, so her purchasing power held. Ruth's period had a small loss. Carl's period, starting in 1966, had high inflation, so his income bought less than half of what it did at the start.

4. The animation doesn't state any advice, but a viewer would likely take away that a fixed or slightly rising payout can lose a lot of real value. That would make them think about inflation risk when choosing between payout options, for example a level payout versus one that adjusts for inflation. A 64-year-old comparing annuity quotes could take that from it.

5. That advice is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the crate counts and says the data is history, not a forecast. It never tells the viewer to choose one option over the other.
